title: Patient
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 34 of 40
content:
Danse warned me that loving him would require patience.

I told him I had already survived his coffee.

He did not find this sufficiently reassuring.

We were in bed at Bravo, fully awake despite the late hour. His fingers traced slow patterns over the back of my hand.

“I’m serious.”

“I know.”

“I don’t know what I’m doing.”

“Neither do I.”

“You seem more confident.”

“That’s because I lie.”

He looked at me.

I smiled.

“Sometimes.”

Danse sighed and stared at the ceiling.

“I spent years avoiding close relationships.”

“I noticed.”

“I thought it made me stronger.”

“Did it?”

“No.”

His hand tightened around mine.

“It made me lonely.”

The honesty was quiet.

I turned on my side to face him.

“You don’t have to be good at this.”

“At what?”

“Being loved.”

His eyes flickered.

“That sounds like something people should be good at.”

“Why?”

“Because receiving something badly can damage it.”

“That is the most Danse sentence you’ve ever said.”

“I don’t know whether that’s an insult.”

“It’s affection.”

He considered that.

Then touched my face.

The kiss started softly.

It deepened because we both wanted it to.

Danse paused when my hand slipped beneath the hem of his shirt.

Not pulling away.

Checking.

I looked at him.

“Okay?”

“Yes.”

He swallowed.

“Are you?”

“Yes.”

The tension left his shoulders.

There was desire between us. Strong enough to make breathing difficult. But there was also history, fear, and Danse’s need to know each step belonged to him rather than some script he could not trust.

So we went slowly.

Kisses. Hands. Laughter when his elbow hit the wall. A muttered curse when the blanket tangled around one ankle.

Nothing cinematic.

Everything real.

At one point he stopped with his forehead against mine.

“I need a minute.”

“Take it.”

“You’re not disappointed?”

“No.”

“You don’t have to say that.”

“I know.”

He stared at me.

Then something in him eased.

“Thank you.”

We stayed close until his breathing settled.

Later, when the lights were off, we stayed close and talked until exhaustion won. Neither of us needed to rush the next boundary.

What mattered most was not what happened.

It was what happened after.

Danse did not retreat into himself.

He stayed.

His arm remained around me. His face rested against my shoulder. The bunker was quiet except for the generator and our breathing.

“I expected to feel different,” he said.

“How?”

“I don’t know.”

“More synthetic?”

He laughed softly.

“Maybe.”

“And?”

“I feel…”

He hesitated.

“Safe.”

My throat tightened.

I kissed his hair.

“That sounds terrible.”

“Don’t ruin it.”

“Wouldn’t dream of it.”

He was silent for a while.

Then, “I’m still going to need patience.”

“I know.”

“And I may say the wrong thing.”

“You absolutely will.”

He lifted his head.

“So will you.”

“Correct.”

“That seems unfair.”

“Terrible system.”

He smiled in the dark.

“Court-martial the designer.”

I laughed quietly.

Danse held me closer.

The armor was gone.

Not forever.

Not completely.

But enough.

The next morning he asked me whether I regretted anything.

Not the night itself.

I could tell by the way he avoided looking at the bed.

Anything.

I sat at the kitchen table wearing one of his shirts because mine was somewhere under a chair.

“Many things.”

Danse’s face fell.

I kicked his ankle gently beneath the table.

“Not that.”

His shoulders lowered.

“You could have specified.”

“You asked an enormous philosophical question before coffee.”

“Fair.”

He poured himself a cup.

I took it away and replaced it with the one I had made.

“Hostile action,” he muttered.

“Humanitarian intervention.”

He drank mine anyway.

For a few minutes we ate quietly.

Then he said, “I regret waiting so long to trust people.”

I looked up.

“Cutler. Haylen. You.”

“You trusted all of us.”

“Operationally.”

“Ah.”

“I kept part of myself separate. I thought if nobody could reach it, nobody could damage it.”

Danse stared into his cup.

“I’m not sure there was anything there. I may have just been making distance and calling it strength.”

I reached across the table.

He took my hand.

“That part was there,” I said.

“How do you know?”

“Because you were protecting it.”

He went quiet.

Later, while we cleaned the bunker, I found the goodbye holotape again.

It had been moved into a drawer with ammunition and spare fuses.

Danse saw it in my hand.

Neither of us spoke at first.

“Do you want it?” I asked.

His face tightened.

“No.”

“Destroy it?”

He thought.

“No.”

I frowned.

“Why keep it?”

“Because I made it.”

He took the tape from me.

“I don’t want to pretend I was never that close to choosing death.”

The words chilled me.

Danse looked at my face.

“I’m not there now.”

“I know.”

“I need you to know that.”

“I do.”

He turned the tape over.

“I thought dying would prove my loyalty.”

“To people who wanted you dead.”

“Yes.”

“That still make sense?”

“No.”

He looked ashamed.

“Some of it does.”

I waited.

“I still understand the impulse. If I could make one clean sacrifice and protect everyone else from uncertainty…”

His mouth tightened.

“That sounds easier than living with the possibility that I might hurt someone someday.”

“Danse.”

“I know.”

He met my eyes.

“That is why I’m keeping the tape. Not as a plan. As evidence of a bad one.”

I exhaled slowly.

“Okay.”

“You trust me with that?”

“Yes.”

The answer scared me.

It was still true.

We placed the tape in a small metal box with his old holotags and the folded list of things he liked.

Not hidden.

Not displayed.

Archived.

Then we went outside because the bunker suddenly felt too small.

The Commonwealth was bright after rain. Water shone on dead grass. Somewhere far off, gunfire echoed and stopped.

Danse took my hand.

“I meant what I said last night.”

“About patience?”

“Yes.”

“You already warned me.”

“I’m warning you again.”

I smiled.

“What exactly am I being warned about?”

“Me.”

“That is vague.”

“I can be rigid.”

“Shocking.”

“Controlling.”

“Sometimes.”

“Difficult to talk to.”

“Often.”

His eyes narrowed.

“I am trying to be vulnerable.”

“I know. Continue.”

He fought a smile.

“I may need reassurance more than I want to admit.”

“Okay.”

“I may also reject it when offered.”

“Infuriating.”

“Yes.”

We had spent the afternoon at the settlement because Danse wanted to practice something he called “normal interaction.”

I told him announcing it that way defeated the purpose.

He disagreed.

At the market, he bought potatoes without interrogating the farmer about storage conditions. He let a child ask about his scar without turning the answer into a safety lecture. He even sat through ten minutes of gossip about a broken engagement and offered no tactical solution.

On the walk home, he looked exhausted.

“Combat is easier,” he said.

“People rarely ask your feelings while shooting at you.”

“Exactly.”

I took his hand.

“Did you hate it?”

“No.”

“Good.”

“I did not understand half of it.”

“That is also normal interaction.”

He squeezed my fingers.

“I keep waiting for you to discover this is more work than you intended.”

There it was.

The real subject beneath patience.

I slowed.

“You are not a project.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

He was quiet.

“I’m trying.”

“That’s different.”

“Yes.”

So I gave him my own list. Not reassurance that he was easy. The truth that I was difficult too.

A little farther down the road, Danse admitted another fear.

“I don’t always know when you need comfort and when you need space.”

“Ask.”

“That simple?”

“No. But the question is.”

He considered.

“And if you don’t know?”

“I’ll tell you that.”

“This seems inefficient.”

“Relationships are not military logistics.”

“I am increasingly aware.”

I squeezed his hand.

“For what it’s worth, I don’t always know either.”

“That does help.”

“Good.”

“Not much.”

“Rude.”

“Honest.”

I laughed.

So did he.

The road home was muddy and slow, which helped. Neither of us could rush the conversation without slipping.

For once, inconvenience was useful.

The settlement lights were already behind us. There was nobody to impress, no mission to complete, and no reason to say any of this except that we wanted the relationship to survive the parts of us that were inconvenient.

I stopped walking and turned toward him.

“And I’m stubborn. I use jokes when I’m scared. I push arguments until they hurt because I hate leaving them unresolved. I sometimes think caring gives me permission to interfere.”

Danse considered.

“Yes.”

“Hey.”

“You requested honesty.”

“Rude.”

His thumb moved over my hand.

“So we both have work.”

“Apparently.”

“That doesn’t sound romantic.”

“It is to me.”

He looked at me.

“Why?”

“Because I don’t want a relationship that only survives while neither of us is difficult.”

Danse’s expression softened.

He leaned down and kissed me beneath a dripping tree.

Slowly.

No panic.

No need to prove anything about bodies or souls.

When we separated, he touched his forehead to mine.

“Patient,” he said.

“Trying.”

“That’s on the list.”

“It is now.”

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
